title: NP versus coNP
formal:
Do there exist a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and constants \(C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every explicitly encoded Boolean CNF formula \(F\),
\[F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\ |\pi|\le C(|F|+1)^k\ \text{ and }\ V(F,\pi)=1?\]
In addition, require soundness on certificates of every length: \(V(F,\pi)=0\) for every satisfiable \(F\) and every binary string \(\pi\). Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\)? All constants and the verifier are fixed independently of the formula.
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes a value in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation; a clause is a disjunction of literals; a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the variables occurring in the formula makes every clause true. The empty clause is false and the conjunction of no clauses is true. Unsatisfiability means that every assignment fails.

Use an explicit binary list of clauses and their signed, binary-encoded variable identifiers, with self-delimiting lengths. The size \(N=|F|\) counts every occurrence, identifier and delimiter. Identifiers may be large integers; assignments need specify only the distinct variables actually occurring, whose number is at most \(N\). There is no circuit, compressed formula or oracle representation of an exponentially large list of clauses. Any fixed efficiently interconvertible explicit encoding gives the same target. Malformed encodings are rejected.

A certificate \(\pi\) is an arbitrary finite binary string, not a derivation in a preselected proof calculus. The verifier is a fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine program with ordinary bit operations and finite-alphabet tapes. There are constants \(D,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), independent of both inputs, such that it halts on every pair in at most \(D(N+|\pi|+1)^d\) steps. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, interaction or uncharged primitive solving another problem. Soundness forbids every accepted certificate for a satisfiable formula, including certificates longer than the proposed short-proof bound. Completeness requires at least one short accepted certificate for each unsatisfiable formula; neither uniqueness nor an efficient algorithm to find it is required. One can reject overlong certificates without changing the existence question.

For a language \(A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\) means that \(x\in A\) exactly when some certificate of length polynomial in \(|x|\) is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class \(\mathrm{coNP}\) consists of complements, within \(\{0,1\}^{*}\), of NP languages. The language of valid unsatisfiable CNF encodings is coNP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: a reduction computes one instance whose yes/no answer is preserved. Consequently its membership in NP is equivalent to the displayed class equality. The family of all possible short certificates may be exponentially large; polynomial verification time is measured on one supplied certificate.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\) or of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), with the stated machine, encoding and resource definitions. For the certificate formulation, an affirmative answer must supply \(V,C,k,D,d\) and prove total polynomial-time verification, soundness for every formula and certificate, and short-certificate completeness for every unsatisfiable formula. A negative answer must show that for every sound polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and every \(C,k\ge1\), there is an unsatisfiable formula \(F\) for which all certificates of length at most \(C(|F|+1)^k\) are rejected. The verifier in this universal statement need not already be a complete proof system. A formulation through complexity classes must also justify the equivalence to the concrete target. Lower bounds for one proof calculus, a fixed polynomial bound, or a chosen verifier do not establish the universal negative statement. Efficient proof search is not required for an affirmative answer. This is an exact yes/no question, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

importance.reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\) and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target.

Haken proves an exponential resolution lower bound for pigeonhole formulas; Buss gives polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system.

The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

context_blocks.text: A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.

sentences: NP asks for short efficiently checkable evidence that an input is a yes instance.
coNP describes the corresponding evidence for no instances of NP problems.
The concrete target asks whether every unsatisfiable CNF formula has a polynomial-length certificate accepted by one fixed sound verifier.
The verifier may use any proof format, and the question does not require efficiently finding a certificate.
Separating the classes requires excluding all such verifiers, beyond lower bounds for individual proof systems.
